paragraphs.text: Perhaps the title of the psalm you heard read has troubled many of you: that Nathan the prophet came to him when he had gone in to Bathsheba. At the same time, the Gospel reading that has just been gone through may have raised no small doubt among the unlearned. In it you noticed that an adulteress was brought to Christ and was sent away without condemnation. Certainly anyone who listens to these things carelessly runs into a temptation to error. He reads of a holy man's adultery and of an adulteress's acquittal, and so slips by an example that is almost human and divine at once: a man thought adultery was something to be done, and God judged that adultery was not to be condemned. Slippery, then, is the road to a fall, whether through pardon or through desire.

Add to this that it seems to kindle the very torches of youthful wantonness, since he did not blush at his adultery or hide it, but published it by proclaiming it in a divine song. What then? Was holy David so shameless and so heedless as to sing his own disgrace? Especially when he himself said in another psalm, which was also gone through today: "How long, Lord, how long shall sinners glory?" Does he forbid others to glory in sin, and then glory in it himself in a sacred song? How, then, are we to sort these things out?

But grant that David went wantonly astray. Did Christ go astray too, so that we should think his judgment was not right? It is fitting, then, that David prophesied today as if to such people, saying: "Understand, you senseless ones, and you fools, be wise at last." For how could Christ err? It is not right that such a thought should even enter our minds. "He who planted the ear, does he not hear? Or he who formed the eye, does he not see? He who rebukes the nations, will he not reprove, he who teaches man knowledge?" Was Christ, then, unable to question guilt and to hear a just accusation? Could Christ approve of wantonness? Did Christ, who rebukes the nations, think that the adulteress need not be reproved? Christ, who knows the inner depths of every heart and teaches the knowledge of the law: could he be deceived by an error, or judge against the order of the law? And then how did he himself say: "I have not come to abolish the law but to fulfill it"? Could Christ, who condemns hidden things, overlook what was public? Can Christ, who made the times, be ignorant of the times? Does he who knows the vain thoughts of men not know their criminal ones too?

Let this, then, be answer enough to those who, though they cannot deny the Creator, still deny the Creator's power; who, while they acknowledge his wisdom, assert his folly by charging him with ignorance of what is to come. I could discuss this at greater length, but a different discourse seems to have been set before us. And although a series of different readings has been gone through, they all serve the same argument, especially the title of the psalm and the Gospel reading. Yet although a single argument unites them, let the order of the discourse follow the order of the readings. So it seems we should first deal with the title of the psalm.

A story has been set before us that contains adultery and murder. For we find it written in the Book of Kings that King David, while walking about in his house, saw the wife of Uriah bathing, at once fell in love with her, and ordered her to be summoned. Then he ordered her husband, an innocent man, as Scripture presents him, to be thrown against the fiercest warriors, so that he would be overwhelmed by the enemy's force. These things were done, and they are not denied. How, then, will they be defended? The Gospel reading gives good advice: even when the sin is plain, the judge's judgment must be sober, and each person must remember his own condition and deserts. For often in judging, the sin of the judgment is greater than the sin of the one who was judged. Some of the wise men of this world have laid down that in judging one should take care that the penalty is not greater than the fault, and this is observed. How much more, then, should this be observed: that whoever is about to judge another should first judge himself, and not condemn lesser errors in another when he himself has committed graver ones. Who are you, then, to judge David, a holy man? I say this to the pagan, I say it to the Jew, I say it to the Christian. And so I think this discourse should be divided into three parts: one against the pagans, another against the Jews, and a third addressed to Christians.

My first address, then, is against the pagans, who commonly raise this objection: "Look how the Christians pursue innocence, profess faith, revere religion, teach chastity, when their leaders are reported to have committed both murders and adulteries! David himself, from whose line, as you say, Christ chose to be born, himself sang of his murders and adulteries. What sort of disciples can they be, who have such teachers?" What then?

Do we deny the deed, or reject the teacher? Neither. But let the one who raises a particular case consider what is common to all. The particular deed belongs to a nature we all share. It is no wonder, then, if the particular falls within the general. For I acknowledge that David was a man, and that is no wonder: I acknowledge what is common, that a man sins. Nor is the weakness of the human condition anything new; it would seem more of a wonder for a man to be free of sin than for him to fall into sin. So holy David did sin; I will not hold you in any doubt. He committed adultery; he contrived a murder, and he both contrived it and carried it out. He sinned as kings are wont to do, but he did penance and wept, as kings are not wont to do. He asked for pardon, not arrogant in his power but conscious of his weakness. Prostrate on the ground, he covered himself with sackcloth, forgetting his royal authority and remembering his guilt.

Find me a man like this: one who, placed in power, does not rather cherish his crimes, proclaim his fault, and defend his sins; one who thinks that what is unbecoming is not permitted to him; who binds himself by his own laws and recognizes that what justice does not permit is not permitted by power either. For power does not set justice aside; rather, justice sets power aside. The king is not set free from the laws; rather, he sets the laws free by his example. Or can it be that

one who judges others is himself free from his own judgment, and takes upon himself what he binds others with? David, then, was good, and far more admirable for having conquered power than if he had conquered love. For chastity is sometimes surrendered to the body, often through error; but power is subject to God, and it is easier for someone to restrain himself in love than to moderate himself in power. Will you not, then, pardon the lesser failing in one in whom you admire greater things? Nature is slippery in all men and prone to sin; slippery too, even where morals are good, is the license of power and the opportunity it offers. For "the anger of a king differs not from the anger of a lion, and whoever provokes him and meddles with him sins against his own soul." Let no one, then, provoke power, lest the soul, entangled in the nets of the body, be unable to free itself from vice. It is no wonder, then, if David too fell under the appearance of power, but much more to be admired that he was called back by the contemplation of faith.

You see, then, that this worldly power often does no good and generally does harm; for guilt often finds its outlet in the authority of power. So you, whatever king you may be, do not presume on your power and resources, for "the heart of the king is in the hand of the Lord." Do not flatter yourself on the subjection of peoples, because "a king will not be saved by the greatness of his strength, nor will a giant be saved by the greatness of his strength." For the Lord takes pleasure not in lofty pinnacles of tents or in costly rooftops, but in those who fear him and in those who hope in his mercy.

We see, then, that power is slippery toward vice; yet I would not say it is always bent that way, since we read that David, though exalted by royal power, increased the worship of God, and that Solomon consecrated a temple to the Lord.

Now let us establish what we touched on briefly, that the opportunity to command is an incitement to sin, and let us follow the order of the story. David would not have violated the rights of another man's bed and the pledges of a sworn marriage had he not seen the woman naked and bathing from the inner part of his house. And so it is well written: "Do not fall for a woman's beauty, and do not desire a woman"; and elsewhere: "Beware of every shameless eye." Do not presume at all on your own self-control and virtue. For "the fornication of a woman will be known by the haughtiness of her eyes and by her eyelids." So first flee the cause of sin, for no one is strong for long. And this is said not only to the weak but to every man: "Let not desire for beauty overcome you" (if you do not want to be overcome, do not engage with sins, lest vices be crowned for victory over you) "and do not be captured by her eyes or carried off by her eyelids." A woman seems to you cheap in price, but she is strong in leading to vice, because "a woman captures the precious souls of men."

It is difficult, then, for anyone entangled in the allurements of lust to escape unharmed. Nor is this judged difficult only in my opinion; in the Proverbs of holy Solomon it is judged impossible. Led by his own example, he says: "Will anyone bind fire in his bosom and not burn his clothes? Or will anyone walk on coals of fire and not burn his feet?" Beware, then, that you too do not kindle the fire of lust and love within the bosom of your mind, lest the garment of your body be consumed by that burning of the soul, and the everlasting life of the resurrection, or at least the footstep of your mind, be scorched, if you think you must walk among the torches of lust. For whoever burns in heart is consumed in body.

In every way, then, encounters with a woman's wantonness must be avoided. And so it says: "Acquire prudence as your pupil, so that she may guard you from another man's wife and from the harlot," lest she hold you bound in the snares of her lips and entangle you in the curls of error. The prophet has therefore taught you where you must guard against the harlot: you must beware of her entry through the window. For she enters by the window of her house, and her window is the eye. So "beware of every shameless eye," lest love come in through the window and lust make its way inside. For the harlot entices her lover by sight, and unless you restrain the wanton gaze of mind and soul, "death enters through the window." The harlot's wantonness is not idle, her lasciviousness not leisurely; it makes the hearts of young men fly, so that they cannot keep their minds steady and are swept this way and that by burning love. Beware, then, of such a woman, "whose feet are never at rest, who wanders abroad and lies in wait at the corners." She binds with her eyes, entices with her words; "she has woven her bed with bands and spread it with tapestries from Egypt." For she takes her adornment not from the knowledge of God but from worldly allurement. With good reason she says her husband is away, since no adulterous woman can

have Christ present. You see, then, by how many nets even the hearts of the saints are caught, and so do not wonder if even holy David was caught: a great man indeed, who by faith conquered the Philistine, huge of body and bristling with weapons of war. But if only he had conquered himself! If only, as he laid that adversary low, he had been able to lay low and overcome the adversary within him! Harder is the fight of one who battles within than of one who battles without.

But why do I speak of David alone? Let us call others too into this discussion, so that we do not think it was the weakness of David, that is, of one man, rather than the frailty of our bodily condition. Samson, mighty and strong, strangled a lion, but he could not strangle his own love. He broke the bonds of his enemies, but did not break the chains of his own desires. He set fire to others' harvests, and he himself, set alight by the spark of one woman, lost the harvest of his strength. Solomon built a temple for God; if only he had kept the temple of his own body! But let my discourse return to the one from whom it turned aside. David triumphed over ten thousands, but he erred against twenty thousands and more; and because he erred, he recognized that he was a man, confessed his fault, and begged for pardon, saying to the Lord: "Lord, do not rebuke me in your anger, nor chasten me in your wrath. Have mercy on me, Lord, for I am weak." If David was weak, are you strong? If Solomon fell, are you immovable? If Paul was the first of sinners, can you be the first of saints? So if these men erred, they erred as men, but they acknowledged their sin as righteous men. If the righteous received a sentence of harsher punishment, how can you hold out to yourself a hope of going unpunished, when Scripture says: "If the righteous man is scarcely saved, where will the sinner and the ungodly appear?"

You notice, then, my children, how often an occasion for sin overturns even a good resolve, and so you must first flee and avoid the occasions themselves. You do not want to be captured by love? Do not gaze at a woman's beauty, because "when your eyes see a strange woman, then your mouth will speak perverse things, and you will lie as if in the heart of the sea, and like a helmsman in a great storm." For the multitude of desires stirs up a great storm, tossing this way and that the one who sails, as it were, on the strait of the body, so that his mind cannot be its own helmsman, and in the fog of love he cannot tell day from night.

Lust, then, is aroused by the eyes, but it is set ablaze by drunkenness; and "every drunkard and fornicator will become poor." Do not flatter yourself on your capacity for drink. Noah became drunk, and he who was not drowned by the flood was overcome by wine. But he did not know the nature of wine, for he had never drunk before; you have learned from him what you must beware of. Lot was deceived through sleep; and if you do not want to be deceived, shake off the sleep of your mind, lest a son mock you when you are drunk, or a daughter deceive you while you sleep. It is not piety that is mocked there, but drunkenness; and it is not a father who is tricked there, but a sleeper. You do not want to be burned? Do not go near the fire. You do not want to be thrown headlong? Flee what is tottering, beware of steep places, keep away from what is about to fall.

You see, then, that in those who were found worthy to be righteous, it was not their nature that was different but their discipline. For after the first man's fall and the just sentence, when the appetite of the flesh was condemned in one man, our condition contracted a fault and guilt infected our nature; but faith tempered the fault of nature itself, and earnest devotion softened the offense.

Turn, then, to God, you nations, and know that the Lord himself is God. He made us, and not we ourselves. Know that we are flesh and dust. Let us therefore leave behind what we have done and revere him who made us, who gave life and forgave sins, who alone can say: "I am, I am he who blots out your iniquities, and I will not remember them." Great indeed is God, and merciful, who confers a benefit and does not reproach us with the gift. Are you surprised that he made David a king and the conqueror of many nations? This is how he is accustomed to raise up his humble servants. He is not stingy with gifts, nor sparing in kindness, nor narrow in grace, nor thrifty; rich in generosity, he enriches with reward those whom he has redeemed from sin. So much against the pagans.

But since we promised a threefold division of this discourse, one part against the pagans, another against the Jews, and a third addressed to the Church, it now seems we must speak against the Jews. Let us review, then, what has been set before us. The title of the psalm says: "Of David, for understanding, when Nathan the prophet came to him, when he had gone in to Bathsheba." This story clearly presents David as both an adulterer and a murderer; and this is the man whom you, Jews, say is the Son of God! But God is the God of virtues, not of crimes, and of his Son God the Father says: "His throne is like the days of heaven." One who has practiced deceit has not overcome sins [?]; and how is it written: "No one is without sin except God alone"? If, then, he who is the Son of God cannot fail to be God, surely the Son of God is the judge of righteousness, not one liable to guilt.

By what notion, then, do you judge either David or Solomon to be the Son of God? Is it because it is written: "O God, give your judgment to the king and your righteousness to the king's son," and because the title of the seventy-first psalm says it was composed for Solomon? But notice which Solomon it means. For Solomon means "peaceable"; that is what the name signifies. The psalm is spoken of him whom we truly know to be a lover of peace. But how was Solomon peaceable? Does not the blood of Joab show otherwise, whom he ordered to be killed among the altars of the temple? Or the punishment of Adonijah, whom he struck down as guilty of seeking a marriage alliance with the royal house, and whom he would not spare from his anger even at his mother's entreaty? And how do you think it fits Solomon, the son of David, when it is written that "he will endure with the sun and before the moon for ages of ages," seeing that he was granted the use of a short life and passed his span of living within narrow limits? And how is it said of him: "He will rule from sea to sea," when he was confined within Syria, that is, held the borders of his rule within the bounds of a single region, whereas Christ alone has extended his rule to the ends of the whole world? For he alone is the one of whom the course of the psalm rightly prophesied that "the kings of the Arabians and of Sheba will bring gifts, and all the kings of the earth will worship him; all nations will serve him." For we know him as ruling all peoples and nations with a rule without bounds and a power without end.

Solomon, then, is not the Son of God. But on what grounds did you think him the Son of God? Because he was wise? But he asked for wisdom, so as to receive what he did not have; Christ is wisdom itself, possessing by nature and in its fullness what Solomon received by grace in human affairs. Indeed, what is received at a point in time is possessed within time. Solomon neither had wisdom at his beginning nor possessed it at his end. For he did not believe he had what he asked for, and afterward, turning away from the worship of God, he fell not as a wise man but as a fool, so that he gave offense; and he did offend, so that he lost even what he had earned. Why, then, did you believe him to be the Son of God? Because he built a temple for God? But that should have led you to believe he was not Lord and God, for it is written: "Unless the Lord builds the house for himself, those who build it have labored in vain." He who built that temple, which fire set beneath it burned down, labored in vain. Or is it because it was said to David his father: "You shall not build me a house, but when you have fallen asleep, I will raise up your offspring after you"? But there too it is not a bodily or material temple that is promised; for God does not dwell in things made by hand. The temple is the holy Church, which is founded not by human but by heavenly power.

For if we are to admire works of a power that is outstanding, yet still human, we find many such men whom we can compare with Solomon. And so where there is equality of works, there is no supremacy of power. Nor can we speak of many sons of God, since we read of one Son of God; and his own benefits, which he bestowed on our fathers, must not be made an occasion to wrong the Son of God. There were many illustrious men, but it was through one, Jesus son of Nun, that it was said: "Let the sun stand still over Gibeon." You see that he advanced beyond David in power, for David ruled over earthly things, not over the stars. You see too that the sun is a servant, not a lord, since it obeyed even a human voice. Yet it stood still because in Jesus it recognized both the type and the name of the one to come. For Jesus son of Nun commanded the heavenly lights not by his own power but by the mystery of Christ. It signified that the Son of God would come into this world, who by divine power would delay the setting of the world's light as it was going down and already sinking into darkness, would give back light, and bring in brightness. Enoch too was taken up to heaven; but he was taken up, while Christ returned. He was taken up lest wickedness should change his heart; Christ abolished the very wickedness of this world. Elijah went up to heaven with chariot and horses, but Christ came down from heaven without chariot or horses. Elijah went up that way because he could not have done so otherwise; Christ went back by his own power. Elisha ordered a leper to wash in the Jordan so as to be cleansed of all contagion; Christ in the Jordan washed the whole world clean. Moses himself, to whom the people of the Jews was entrusted so that they might cross over, divided the water. He did indeed divide the elements, because he did not divide the power of the Trinity; he separated the masses of water because he did not separate the Father from the Son.

You see how great these men were, and what proofs of their deeds they left behind. How then can you judge those whom you recognize as equal in power to King David or Solomon to be unequal in standing, so that you think Solomon, David's son, sits at God's right hand? This is especially so when David himself plainly showed of whom the words were spoken. For he would not say of his own son: The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand. How could he call his own son lord? The law forbids it, religion resists it, and faith recoils from it, that you should place a mortal man at the right hand of almighty God. The one who sits at the right hand is another: he who took on a body, not he who began from a body. He was begotten before the morning star, that is, before the brightness of all lights, since he himself created the brightness of the various lights; Solomon certainly comes after the morning star. Solomon was not a priest. Therefore almighty God could not say to him: From the womb, before the morning star, I begot you. It could not be said to him: You are a priest for ever according to the order of Melchizedek, especially since in the time when Solomon lived the priests were according to the order of Aaron, not of Melchizedek. For the priests were still offering the blood of goats and bulls for the sins and errors of the people. But after he came who offered himself for the salvation of the world, so that the blood of Christ might wash clean those whom the blood of bulls could not cleanse, the priests began to offer themselves as victims.

And so with a single question our Lord Jesus Christ stopped the mouths of all the heretics and shut in their sacrileges. By this question he refuted not only the Jews but also the Photinians, the Arians and the Sabellians. And so, since we now see that the Jews have fallen away and that their accursed faithlessness has dwindled, in treating this question we must now touch briefly on the Arians, who differ little from the Jews, and on the Photinians and Sabellians. Let Photinus be silent, then, who says that Christ is the son of David and not of God; let him be silent, condemned by a heavenly voice. For how can he say that Christ is David's son, when David himself said in the book of Psalms: The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand, until I put your enemies beneath your feet? If David, he says, calls him Lord, how is he his son? Christ, then, is not David's son but God's Son. Let the Sabellian be silent too. When he reads that the Lord spoke to the Lord, let him understand that the one who speaks and the one spoken to are not one and the same. For the Father does not say to himself: Sit at my right hand, nor did he say to himself: I will put your enemies. Let them all at last understand that it is the Son who sits at the right hand, and let them keep this distinction between Father and Son: the Father is one and the Son is another. But because they sit on one throne and possess one majesty, and sit not to mark a difference of rank or an order of power but in the bond of love, let them understand that the Father and the Son have one power. Here let Arius also fall silent, who presses on in the tracks of the error opposite to that of Sabellius. Let him hear the Lord speak to the Lord, let him hear that the Son sits at the Father's right hand, and let him stop raising questions about the Godhead from human speech and human ranking. Nor let him argue here from the fact that the Father says 'Sit'. For elsewhere we read that the Son sits even without the Father's word, as it is written: And he sits at the right hand of God, and elsewhere: From now on you will see the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of God. The one to whom 'Sit' is said is the very one who is called the Son of Man. He hears as man; he sits as the Son of God. What could be called more excellent than this power, which placed even human flesh at God's right hand, and, once the Word had become flesh, joined that weakness of the human condition to the eternal Godhead? But what is this?

Now that Photinus has been struck dumb, Arius has fallen silent and Sabellius has lost his voice, I still see other mouths stirring up heresy against the Church. For look: the Manichaean, the Valentinian and every offshoot of the Manichaeans rely on the very weapon by which the others were slain. Their heresy contrives a prejudice against the faith out of the testimony of the faith. For that detestable heresy says: 'See, Christ denied that he was the son of David; therefore,' it says, 'we must believe that he did not take flesh.' Scripture answers them most plainly at the very beginning of the Gospel, saying: The book of the genealogy of Jesus Christ, the son of David. Why then is he called the son of David in one place and denied to be the son of David in another, unless it is so that you may understand that to be a son according to the divine substance is one thing, and to be a son by taking on flesh is another? According to the divine substance he is the Son of God; according to the flesh he is the son of David. So where the Saviour's generation according to the flesh is described, he is called the son of David; but where the fullness of confession is demanded, when the Saviour's [divine] generation is set forth, the Son of God does not wish to be called the son of David, for the title that marks his majesty expresses his nature. But now that the interpretations of the perverse have been refuted, our discourse must turn to the Church.

That we so often return to the title of the fiftieth psalm is a sign not of presumption but of weakness. Whether through the limits of my ability or the frailty of my voice, I cannot complete the whole course of the treatise in a single day. On the previous day our discourse was directed against the Jews. The proofs of the faith pressed them so far that Christ was placed on the heavenly throne, which certainly cannot befit a mere man, since it is not credible that anyone but the Son of God sits at God's right hand. With every ambiguity removed, then, we must hold that none other sits at the Father's right hand than the Son of God. Again, since Scripture says: Of the fruit of your womb I will set upon your throne, we must surely believe that the same Son of God took flesh from Mary. In that flesh is the fruit of the womb of which the prophet spoke, so that you may truly recognize the line of descent and not doubt that he, the Son of God, who afterward became the Son of Man by taking flesh, sits on the heavenly throne. For Christ had no royal throne in this world that would lead you to think some other throne was promised to David's seed, especially since the Lord himself said: My kingdom is not of this world.

Hemmed in on every side, then, they turn the efforts of their faithlessness to this: they assert that it is incredible that God took flesh, yet they cannot explain why he could not have taken it. I ask whether they think God could not take flesh because it was impossible or because it was beneath him. If because it was impossible, is anything then impossible for God? There is nothing he has willed to do and could not do. It remains, then, to show whether he willed it or not. And what greater sign of his will could there be than his own words: I appeared openly to those who did not seek me; I stretched out my hands to a people that does not believe and speaks against me? If, then, he willed it and was able, are we to think that he refused because it would be an indignity? What indignity can the Godhead feel? It is beyond the reach of insult and is not subject to our passions, for flesh could bring the Godhead neither loss nor gain.

Those who object that the Son of God could not take flesh: if they are pagans, how can they say this, when they testify that their gods were seen in human form, since they cannot deny that those gods were men? Could their king, whom they set above all their gods, take on monstrous shapes for the sake of a love affair, while Christ could not take on, for the salvation of the world, the flesh of man, whom he made in his own image, that most excellent work of his? Does it seem finer to them that a bodily form was assumed in order to commit adultery with another man's wife than for the redemption of all? And if a Jew raises this objection, how does he read: Behold, a virgin shall conceive in the womb and bear a son, and his name shall be called Emmanuel, which means 'God with us'? How does he read: Behold, I who spoke am here? And how does he claim to read: Behold, like a panther and like a bear robbed of its young I will fall upon them? Could the Son of God, then, not take flesh for the redemption of all, when they themselves cannot deny that, to punish our sins, God put on something like the cruelty of a wild beast, so that he who is by nature kind and merciful, stirred by the atrocity of our crimes, takes on a kind of bestial savagery against us?

But since I think that enough answer has now been given to the Jews, both yesterday and today, I must now give you, dearest brothers, an account of the prophetic deed. When the title of this psalm was first read, that Nathan came to David when he had gone in to Bathsheba, we said that very many people are offended by the course of this story. So we undertook a threefold treatment of it, and I thought the treatment should be divided as follows. Before the pagans, the fall that belongs to our condition should not be denied, but the correction of the error should be established. Before the Jews, we should teach that holy David fell so that the faithlessness of the Jews might stumble no longer, and they would stop believing that one to be the Son of God whom they saw subject to sin through the common condition. And Christians should be able to perceive the mysteries of the rising Church. So the division was threefold: one according to nature, another according to faith, the third according to grace. Weakness does not shut a man out from pardon, faith excuses him from guilt, and the sacraments secure the grace that was promised long ago.

Granted that David sinned: he sinned so that the whole world might not go astray. He sinned against himself so that he might correct us all. Finally, he sinned against his own body (for he who commits fornication sins against his own body); he sinned against his own body so that he might be redeemed in the body of Christ. See: the man we thought could scarcely be defended, we now see must be praised. For who would not rather have the divine gifts in him proclaimed than his human works? For we hold, with the Apostle, that a man is justified by faith without the works of the law. Let David, then, be justified by faith: through the law he recognized his sin, but by faith he believed in pardon for sin. Let David be justified, because in his sin the mysteries of the Church that was to rise shone forth.

Someone will ask why a man chosen to be an ancestor of the Lord's line committed both adultery and murder. But I say something else: it was precisely such a man who had to be chosen as an ancestor of the Lord's body. For what is the incarnation but the forgiveness of sins? And so he could not be free of sin, so that he might display divine grace both by his example and by his message. Indeed, it was by the same design that Bathsheba and Tamar are counted among the ancestors of the Lord's line, one of whom committed adultery and the other incest. By the same design Ahab and Jeconiah, as Matthew the evangelist recorded, are numbered among Christ's forebears, so that he who was to redeem all men might begin his kindness with his own ancestors. It was also so that he who submitted even to bodily suffering might not seem to have sought the nobility of a spotless descent; for it is human vanity to seek glory that belongs to others and not to oneself, and yet even among men the grace of virtue counts for more than that of nobility. At the same time an example had to be given, so that all might understand that the disgraces of ancestors cannot dishonour their descendants, since each person can wipe out the stain of his line by the merit of his own virtue. Do you see how many people, and how grievous their crimes, the line of the Lord's descent includes, and yet Christ did not blush to be born of their stock for your sake? If you believe this, these are gifts of divine mercy toward you, and this is the mark of heavenly power; for sin abounded so that grace might abound all the more. So David was not exempt from guilt, in order that he might be chosen for grace.

But now let us review the mysteries of the story itself and draw from the very springs of the Scriptures. So that we may look into the whole sequence of mysteries, let us repeat the text of the story itself. We remember that it is told like this in the book of Kings. David saw Bathsheba, the wife of Uriah, bathing, and fell in love with her; then he ordered her to come to his house while the woman's husband was away. Not long afterward her husband came back as a messenger from the war. He was a truly religious and devoted man, who thought that he ought not to enter his house in time of war, when he saw his comrades intent on battle and keeping watch not in their homes but in their battle tents. Afterward, by David's order, he was sent back to the war with the instruction that he be thrown in the way of the enemy fighters, so that by the husband's death the king might be free to possess the woman. Even here there is some shame at the sin and embarrassment at the guilt: he looked for a hiding place for his wrongdoing, and instead of claiming authority for an unjust killing by right of royal power, he tried to avoid the odium of it. I admit the guilt, but a fault weighed down by shame is more bearable than one paraded with insolence. So Uriah died, thrown in the way of the enemy fighters; but afterward the very men who had killed him were themselves put to death by David's order when their city was stormed. This is the course of the story, and in it one may behold deep mysteries.

We have undertaken not to defend David, for he needs no help of mine, but to excuse him, or rather to praise him. So, lest I falter in so great a depth of mysteries, it is right that I should use the words of the man whose story I am using. I will use, then, the prophet's response, saying: Create a clean heart in me, O God, and renew a right spirit within me. For no one can behold such hidden depths of the divine mystery without the outpouring of the Holy Spirit. If so great a prophet asks that the gift of the Holy Spirit be poured into him, what must I, weak as I am, do? This is all the more so since even the holy Apostle asks to be helped by the people's prayers, that a door may be opened to him to speak the mystery of the word. O that Christ would deign to open that door to me! Yet let us knock, for he always hears those who knock, since he himself said: Knock, and it will be opened to you. O that he would open himself to me, for Christ is the door! He is within and he is without; he is the way that leads us, and he is the life we strive to reach.

Come, then, Lord Jesus, and open your springs to us, that we may drink of the water which whoever drinks will never thirst again. Or, if we cannot yet draw from your spring, grant that we may at least draw from the well, from which you promised drink to that Samaritan woman while she was still doubting. You promise drink from the spring to all, but to those who doubt, like that Samaritan woman, your spring is still a deep well. Let us too drink the water of heavenly secrets, and since we have been found worthy to come to your spring, may we at least see an image of the heavenly mysteries.

So, unless I am mistaken, by the prophet we shall understand the Holy Spirit, and by the adulteress we may take the various fornications of the synagogue to be meant. And so we see it revealed long beforehand that the Lord Jesus would be born of the Holy Spirit and of the family of the Jews, to whom belong the fathers, from whom Christ came according to the flesh. As a Jew he was born of an adulterous family, but as the spotless one he was born of a virgin. The family of the Jews was under the law as if under a husband. The observance of the law had to be abolished, so that truth and grace might take its place.

We have one mystery; now receive another. But remember that from Bathsheba's first conception a little child was born who died, and afterward Solomon was born: the little child from a stolen conception, but Solomon from an acknowledged marriage. It is clear, then, that by David we are to understand the prophet, and by the prophet the prophetic people, from which the synagogue also came. The first child who was born is the Jewish people. Because it fell away from its ancestors, formed through shameful deeds and conceived through vices, it could not reach the age of resurrection or grow up into a perfect man, but failed in a meagre smallness of understanding and a kind of infancy of virtue. But the one conceived afterward from a lawful union is the Christian people, the wise and peaceful one (for this is what the meaning of Solomon's name discloses), and it has reached the white-haired age of a long-lived resurrection and that heavenly kingdom. Through the former people the law was dissolved; through the latter, grace was restored.

Receive a third mystery as well. The name the Hebrews call David is interpreted in Latin as 'humbled'. And who is truly humbled but he who did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped, but, taking the form of a servant, humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death? He, then, is the one signified by David: exalted by nature but humbled by mercy, lofty in his Godhead but meek in his body. So where he is humbled, there he is obedient. For obedience springs from the same source as humility, and ends in it. When he is said to have become obedient unto death, the death not of the Godhead but of the body, that obedience was surely not of the Godhead but of the body, and that humility was not of the majesty but of the flesh. So, as regards the taking of the body, the reading from the Apostle has shown in what Christ's humility consisted. What concerns the nature of the Godhead was disclosed by the Gospel reading, which you greeted with devout assent when you heard the Son of God say in it: I and the Father are one. For the Son and the Father are one in Godhead, but the sacrament of the body and the eternity of the Godhead are not one. Yet it was not only the Apostle who said that the Lord was humbled; he himself also declared that he was humble, saying: Take my yoke, for it is light, because I am meek and humble of heart. And he is indicated not only by the meaning of the name but also by explicit mention of it, for it is written: I have found David my servant; with my holy oil I have anointed him; and further on: He shall say to me: You are my Father; and: I will say to him: You are my Son. So we have found the David we were seeking: a servant in appearance, but Lord in truth. This David, then, was walking about inside his house.

And what house is Christ's but the one of which he says: In my Father's house are many dwelling places? Placed, then, in that palace, he saw the human condition naked, and in pity fell in love with it. For it was still naked of virtues, since through the serpent's wiles it had been stripped of the coverings that belonged to its nature. It does not seem likely that a woman would undress in front of the king's house, that a woman would bathe in front of the king's house, as if there could be no better place for a bath. It does not fit, it does not agree, it does not accord with faith; it is far from the truth and repugnant to sense. Such a woman, so wanton and so brazen, the king could only have loathed, not loved. Could she not, if not out of respect for her husband [?], at least have been abashed before the king's gaze? Or could not even his servants have kept her away before the king saw her?

If, then, this cannot accord with faith, let us ask who this naked woman is. Clearly she is the human condition, stripped of all the garments of nature, lacking the cloak of immortality and robbed of the covering of innocence; for whoever is stripped bare by sin and guilt is naked. Indeed, that first sinner of our race, and would that he had been the only one, did not perceive that he was naked before he sinned. After he sinned, he saw that he was naked and so thought he must cover himself with leaves, because he knew that he was naked. He became naked in his own eyes, then, once he had become guilty. In him the whole human condition was stripped bare, liable through the inheritance of nature not only to guilt but also to hardship. So he felt and saw himself naked. Hence our whole condition is such that whoever thinks himself naked both sees and feels himself naked. In short, he who covets riches is naked; he who despises them is rich. So true is it that each man's hardship lies in his own perception, and each man's own virtue is beyond the reach of harm. So Christ first claimed the human condition as his bride through the law, and afterward repudiated her. That is why he says: Where is your mother's bill of divorce, with which I sent her away? In this way, then, Christ saw his household naked and loved it; for Christ loves the holy soul. Indeed, Jesus loved Lazarus and Mary; Christ loved his Church, though she was naked, though she was not yet clothed with any adornment of virtues.

Finally, so that we may know that the course of the Scriptures fits the plan set out before us, let us learn of the Church as naked, let us learn of her as seeking, hastening and washing herself before the house of Christ, at the time when John was baptizing in the Jordan and saying: “I baptize you with water for repentance, but he who comes after me is mightier than I, whose sandals I am not worthy to carry. He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit.” So when the people were being baptized for repentance, they were seeking Christ, being already close to his house, so that they might attain grace. The Church, then, was seeking Christ in John, saying: “Tell me, you whom my soul has loved,” declaring that he himself was the cause of her longing and the cause of her washing, as you have it: “I am dark and comely, daughters of Jerusalem, like the tent of Kedar, like the skin of Solomon.” Here you have the reason why she longs to wash herself: she declares that she is dark. For it is as though John asked why the great crowd that came flocking together longed to be washed, and she answered him, saying: “I am dark and comely, daughters of Jerusalem.” Because she is dark, she desires to be washed; because she is comely, she is not afraid to be seen naked. “Do not look at me,” she says, “because I have been darkened, because the sun has not looked upon me.” So we grow dark when we are not seen by Christ, but when we are seen, we become white. He, then, saw her, he to whom all things are naked and from whom the inner secrets of the heart cannot be hidden, for he is the searcher of heart and reins; nothing is covered from him, nothing is wrapped in concealment. He saw his Church naked, and as soon as he saw her he fell in love with her. He saw his beloved naked, and as the Son of love he loved her.

See how he invites her, see how he calls her. Here there is no shame of adultery, but the mysteries of chastity. “You are all fair,” he says, “my near one, and there is no blemish in you. Come here from Lebanon, my bride, come here from Lebanon; you shall pass and pass through from the beginning of faith.” And rightly “from the beginning of faith.” So where you have faith, you need not fear adultery; for faith belongs to marriage, deceit to adultery. But so that she might be able to come from Lebanon, he first said: “Arise, come, my near one, my fair one, my dove, my perfect one”: near, surely, through her longing for faith; fair through the beauty of virtue; a dove through spiritual grace. For the wings of a dove covered with silver signify that eternal power, and the flight of the dove declared the presence of the Holy Spirit. So Christ calls her to himself, that she may come, since she was now coming endowed with a spiritual dowry, “for behold,” he says, “the winter is past, the rain is over and gone its way, the flowers have appeared in the land.” See how the holy Church is invited. “The winter,” he says, “has gone its way,” so that she, being naked, need not dread the winter: not the winter of the season, but of weakness, which strips the fertile field of the soul of every flower. For there is a winter that does not depend on the earthly sun; there is a winter of the mind, when cold steals into the soul, when the warmth of the spirit fades away, when the vigour of the senses is slackened, when too much moisture overflows and weighs down the mind, when the inner sight grows dim. And that is why the Lord says: “See that your flight be not in winter or on the sabbath.” For it is good that the day of judgment or of death should come at a time when a gentle mildness thrives in the soul, when the heavenly mystery shines with a serene light, when our heart burns within us. For then Christ is present, as Ammaon and Cleopas testify in the Gospel, saying: “Did not our heart burn within us on the road, when he opened the Scriptures to us?” And the soul thrives when a flower too is seen in the land. What is this sweet-smelling flower but he who said: “I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys”? Of him it is also written in Isaiah: “A rod shall come forth from the root of Jesse, and a rod shall rise up from the root, and a flower shall come forth from the rod.” The root, surely, is the family of the Jews, the rod is Mary, and the flower of Mary is Christ. When he shines in our land, gives off his fragrance in the field of the soul, or blossoms in his Church, we cannot fear the cold nor dread the rain, but can await the day of judgment.

And so the Church hastened with all eagerness to see this flower, as she herself testifies, saying: “On my bed by night I sought him whom my soul has loved. I sought him and did not find him; I called him, and he did not hear me. So I will rise and go into the house, into the marketplace and the streets, and I will seek him whom my soul has loved. I sought him and did not find him. The watchmen who go about the city found me; they struck me and took my cloak away from me.” You see how she seeks the one she longs to find, so that she does not fear to be wounded. But these wounds are not to be feared but to be desired,
because they are the wounds of love, as she herself said: "I am wounded by love." Good are the wounds of love. Indeed, "better are the wounds of a friend than the willing kisses of an enemy."

So she is rightly naked, because she has lost her cloak. Or perhaps she is naked because it is sometimes a mark of virtue not to have a covered breast or a veiled heart. Indeed, Christ looked down on and spurned the veiled one, that is, the synagogue. She had a veil over the reading of the Old Testament, and it is not lifted, because it is done away with in Christ. The veiled synagogue, I say, Christ spurned, and that is why to this day a veil lies over the heart of the Jews. But she who turns to the Lord with her whole mind is naked and open to view. For when anyone turns to the Lord, the veil will be taken away, so that, beholding the glory of God, we may be able to see. Elsewhere too, nakedness is a sign of virtue, for it is written: I have put off my tunic; how shall I put it on?

I have washed my feet; how shall I soil them? Let us then uncover from the Scriptures, if we can, what tunic she put off and could not find a way to put on again. For there is a bodily tunic, and there are veils woven out of desires. That is why it is sometimes better to be naked in body than veiled in heart. Hence Paul too tells us that it is much better to be stripped than to be clothed over, and elsewhere he also says: Strip off the old man with his deeds and put on the new, who is renewed in knowledge according to the image of him who created him. So she who has been stripped also has washed feet, and having washed, she does not know how she could be soiled; for through grace she forgets what she had taken in through nature. Great, then, and just is this love for the woman who bathed before David's palace.

But she not only washed; she also called, as we read in the same book, where the holy Church says: Come, my brother, let us go out into the field, let us lodge in the villages, let us rise early for the vineyards, let us see whether the vines have blossomed. So she not only washes but also calls Christ and invites him to come to her, saying: I will give you my breasts. And she promises not only her own breasts but also things new and old, as you have it: New and old, my brother, I have kept for you. And as if she cannot bear her love, she looks for someone's help, someone to ask Christ to come. See her burning, see her longing! Who will give you to me, she says, my brother, nursing at my mother's breasts? She shows why she seeks him, with what grace she invites him and how she can hold him. She shows how she waits for him while he lingers outside, and she begs him to enter her house, saying: Finding you outside, I will kiss you; I will take you and bring you into my mother's house, into the inner chamber of her who conceived me. You see how she is naked, she who can have no covered secret: the secret of a nature wholly undefiled, the secret of an inmost conscience unmarked by any recklessness of vice. For the holy Church is a garden enclosed and a spotless virginity, and she earns this grace from Christ because she sought the Word of God, longed for him and found him, keeping watch before the doors of Wisdom, as Wisdom herself says: Blessed is the man who hears me, the man who keeps my ways, watching daily at my doors and guarding the posts of my entrance; for my goings out are the goings out of life.

So Christ desired the beauty of his Church and prepared to take her to himself as his wife. But because she was under the law (for Peter, John and the rest of the apostles [?] were under the law), he judged that we must first be released from the hooks of bodily observance. The law is indeed devout and just, as the figure of Uriah shows: he was so devout and chaste that on returning from war he would not acknowledge his wife or go in to her. Yet when David, that is, the humble man, came to know Uriah's wife, he was withdrawing from union with the synagogue and preparing a place for the Church's future marriage. Hence John too received the type of the law. Though he came of the fathers, he announced that the ways of the Lord were to be prepared and prophesied the Church's union, and so he is presented as slain, to show the end of the law's observance; for the law and the prophets lasted until John. So Uriah has now been slain as a type of the law, so that the synagogue might be released from the snares of the law. For a woman who is under a husband is bound by the law as long as her husband lives, but if her husband dies, she is released from the law of her husband. So while her husband lives she will be called an adulteress if she is joined to another man; but if her husband dies, she is freed from the law of her husband, so that she is not an adulteress if she is with another man. The human condition, then, is not adulterous: though it was under the law, it has been claimed for grace, now that the observance of the law has in a certain way been abolished.

Yet it was not Christ who abolished the observance of the law. That is why David did not kill Uriah either, but let him be killed by warriors. In other words, Christ allowed the rite of observance that came from the law to be profaned through the invasion of barbarians and the captivity of the Jews. Moreover, Uriah means "my light." And what is Christ's light but the law and the gospel? (For if you believed Moses, you would believe me too, for he wrote of me.) The light of Christ went before in the law, and afterwards in the gospel his grace filled this whole world as though by the sevenfold Spirit. From this law, then, he took away the flesh and joined the Church to himself. The hostile people dimmed the light of this law when they violated its holy things. So the light of God has been dimmed among the Jewish people, because blindness has come upon part of Israel until the fullness of the Gentiles comes in, and so all Israel will be saved.

There still remains a fourth mystery. I ask you to receive it with calm ears and to weigh my meaning, not my words; for the kingdom of God is not in word but in power. Adultery was committed, and murder was committed. This is what was said to the prophet: Take for yourself a rod of walnut. Elsewhere too we read of a walnut rod, by which we understand a certain law and the sum of prophecy. Like a walnut, prophecy is bitter on the outside in its rind, hard in the shell in the middle, and tender and fruitful within. So even if you hear rather bitter things in the history and find hard things in the type, still hope for fruitful things in the mystery. Adultery, I say, was committed as a figure of salvation; for not every adultery is to be condemned. Indeed, it was said to the prophet: Go, take for yourself a wife of fornication. The Lord commands a marriage with a woman who has committed fornication, and the offspring of that marriage, as we said above, is Christ. For the son born of fornication was given the name Jezreel by the Lord, which means divine offspring. If, then, that union with a harlot was holy, this partnership, the union with an adulteress, is certainly holy too. But that concerns the Jews. Concerning divine things, I do not dare to use the word adultery, even holy adultery, lest the mere sound of the word offend anyone, though a more reverent sense lies ready to hand. What can be said more cautiously, if less plainly, is this: from unequal partners a holy union was made when the Word became flesh. For the partnership of divinity and flesh is not a lawful one. Soul and flesh are natures that come together by a kind of covenant, flesh with soul and soul with flesh; but divinity and flesh do not in the same way keep the law of a lawful marriage bed. God took up flesh and assumed a soul, and through an unheard-of and unlawful incarnation he made the partnership lawful, so that God may be all in all.

Finally, so that you may know it is a mystery, interpret the names. You take David as a type of Christ, and Bathsheba means daughter of the sabbath, full daughter, and well of the oath. What could be clearer, then, than that the daughter of the sabbath is the flesh of Christ? For God sent his Son, made of a woman, made under the law. She is also full, because in his passion is the fullness of the law, or because she is full of the Holy Spirit; for Jesus, full of the Holy Spirit, returned from the Jordan. She is also the well of the oath, that is, of religion and faith. And rightly a well, for rivers of living water will flow from his belly. God the Word, then, took her to himself and made the union lawful. This mystery is also declared by the marriage in the Song of Songs, in which the Church is wedded to Christ and the flesh to the spirit. That is why she ran about and sought the Word of God everywhere: wounded, naked, adulterous in all things, though spotless in Christ, the wretched flesh was seeking a redeemer.

Christ joined her to himself in order to make her spotless; he took her as his partner in order to take away her adultery. And because she was under the law, she had to die to be freed from the law, so that through that death a kind of marriage between law and flesh might be dissolved. So the flesh died in Christ, so that we, put to death to the law through the body of Christ, as the apostle said, might belong to another, to him who rose from the dead. Thus the passions and desires of the flesh and the thoughts of sin, which through the law were at work in our members, would die in that death, and we, freed from the law of death, would rise in newness of spirit as in a new union with Christ.

And yet all who dissolved the law in Christ's flesh and thought it should be violated were slain by warriors at David's command. This sign shows what they have taught was marked out for later times: that none of those who killed Christ escaped. It also reveals most clearly that those whom Christ had taken to himself before his death perished like the Jews, as infants still unformed, while those whom he adopted after his death were kept for the kingdom among the number of sons. So in keeping with this mystery it is fitting that the first offspring, among the Jews, was weak, so that afterwards an eternal fruit might come about among Christians.

But now let us move on to the message. Up to this point we have treated the prophet David's notorious adultery and murder. Having gone through the mysteries, we found not only nothing to condemn but even something to praise. Now the treatment of the message begins, which the title of the psalm we have been discussing, often repeated already, points to. It runs thus: A psalm of David, for understanding, when Nathan the prophet came to him, when he had gone in to Bathsheba.

So this part of the history too must be unfolded, and it goes like this. "A rich man and a poor man," he says, "lived in one city. The rich man had many herds and many sheep; the poor man had one sheep, which was fed on his bread and wine and rested in his bosom. A guest came to the rich man. The rich man took nothing from his own herds or flocks, but killed the poor man's one sheep. When David learned of this, he said, 'That man shall die, and he shall restore it fourfold.' Nathan answered him, 'You are the man.'" Then he revealed to him the heavenly command: the Lord declared that he had bestowed many good things on him, that is, royal wealth, after taking him from among the shepherds, and had poured out his mercy on him; and therefore, since he had provoked the Lord by his sin, all he had would be carried off and seized by enemies, and his house would be laid waste. Then David said, "I have sinned," and Nathan answered, "Since you confess that you have sinned, the Lord will forgive your sin; but your son who was born of Bathsheba shall die." When this son fell ill, David wept, lay on the ground, covered himself with sackcloth and fasted. When he learned that the child was dead, he rose, washed, ate, and comforted others.

See how much is here! First of all, God is kind and merciful, and the adversities that befall us we receive as the price of our error. We have learned, then, that captivity is the price of sin, for this is the penalty decreed for the crime. Next we notice that the falls of kings are the punishment of peoples. For just as we are kept safe by their virtue, so we are put in danger by their error. Hence we should pray that we may have a glorious and perfect king. Do we, then, who want a perfect king, refuse to have a perfect Lord? Or can those who refuse to let God be perfect want a man to be perfect? The text of the history also briefly makes us notice how quickly the hope of pardon followed. It is no small thing that it was Nathan who rebuked him, that is, a lesser prophet; for it is a heavy shame and embarrassment to have one's offence rebuked by an inferior. You see that guilt diminishes grace. Nathan knew what David did not know, so dark does the mind become when overshadowed by a cloud of vices. Moreover, this is the same Nathan who earlier prophesied that David was acceptable to the Lord, so that David would grieve to have his sin exposed by the very witness through whose prophecy his merit had been proclaimed.

But now let us look for the mystery. There were two men, he says, in one city, one rich and the other poor. Who are this rich man and this poor man, if not the Jewish people on the one hand and the Christian people on the other? The one is rich in the law, rich in the words of God entrusted to him, rich in prophecies, rich in oracles; the other is poor. But do not flee this poverty, which the kingdom of heaven follows; for it is written: Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven. Good is the poverty that does not lose what it has had. Good is the poverty that, though it has no treasures of money, has treasures of knowledge and wisdom. Do not look down on poverty as something cheap, my children: this poor man cried, and the Lord heard him. Do not envy riches as something great: the rich have been in want and gone hungry. But if you want to have good things, seek the Lord; for those who seek the Lord will lack no good thing. So do not reject any poor man. Peter was poor and had no coin to give, but he gave health, which is more precious than any money. Lazarus in the gospel was poor; but the rich man who once lay in scarlet and purple longed after his life ended to be cooled by a drop from the poor man's finger. Proud in his royal scarlet and purple robes, the fastidious rich man had shuddered at the poor man's sores; yet once placed in hell, he longed to be where Lazarus was. In this passage the reading does not seem to describe a man rich or poor in money, but a poor man who for the sake of faith and devotion did not shudder at the wounds of the body and endured hunger and fasting.

So although the Jewish people had in their flocks great stores of sacrificial victims, they nevertheless seized the one little sheep that the poor people had and subjected it to that glorious passion. Do you want to know which sheep? He who was led like a sheep to the slaughter, who was fed on the poor man's bread, drank the poor man's drink, and slept in the poor man's bosom. For he lived on our food and rested in the lap of our heart. He declared that he could not rest in the bosom of the Jews, saying: The Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head.

And a guest came, he says, to that rich man. Who is this guest, if not wretched sin? For guilt entered this world like a guest, alien and foreign to our nature. So he did not offer a victim from his own flocks, but took the poor man's little sheep and killed it. Though its passion served for the sacrifice that brings salvation, for him it seems to have been only an increase of his fury, food for his guilt and a spur to sin. Thus Judas received bread from Christ and was then filled all the more with the devil, because he did not receive it in faith, since he was plotting betrayal against so hospitable a Lord.

And David was angry with that man. We have said that the prophet represents the Jewish people, and so under this figure he condemns himself. That man who did this deserves death, and he will restore the little sheep fourfold. That is, the Jewish people will perish, but the Christian people will enjoy goods in greater abundance, because the state that is owed from the resurrection surpasses present things.

My purpose, as you will kindly recall, was to answer in my sermon those who condemn holy David's murder and adultery. Thanks to the favour of your united goodwill, the course of my treatise has turned out such that the man we thought could not be defended has seemed to everyone rightly worthy of praise. But since the holy man needs no help from us, let him now speak to you for himself, and let his own words defend his deed.

Have mercy on me, O Lord, he says, according to your great mercy. Unless I am mistaken, dearest brothers, this pairing of words, "great mercy," is new, and I do not easily recall reading it elsewhere. We must therefore consider what great mercy is. For though we do not often read of great mercy, we do read of the great power of God. So by considering what great power is, we will be able to work out what he meant by great mercy. For we read in holy Jeremiah: Who are you, O Lord? You made heaven and earth by your great power and your outstretched arm. Great power, then, made heaven. Whose is this great power, the Father's or the Son's? It is certainly the great power of the Father, for he made heaven and earth through the Son, as you have it: In the beginning God made heaven and earth. But the Son too is great power. For when you read that the Son is the power of the Father, as you have Christ called the wisdom and power of God, then surely, since the Son is the power of the Father, the Son is great power. How then can he be denied to be almighty, when we confess that he is the great power of God? This great power, then, made heaven, because the Son too made heaven, as you have it: All things were made through him. So if both the Father and the Son made it, the oneness of the work surely shows the oneness of their working. The working of the Father and the Son does not differ, then. And if their working is one, then surely the power at work is one and the majesty of the works is one. So much for the Father and the Son.

Why, then, are we silent about the Spirit, especially when divine Scripture does not let us be silent? For this passage provides a most fitting testimony to prove the unity of the Holy Spirit with the Father and the Son, so that we cannot separate his working from the work of the Father and the Son either. We read that the Father is great power, because he made heaven, and that the Son too is great power, since he made heaven; and he not only made it but also established it, for by the word of the Lord the heavens were established. So if both making heaven and establishing it belong to great power, we cannot separate the Holy Spirit from the majesty of great power either, since it is written: And by the Spirit of his mouth all their power. For when heaven and earth were being made, the Spirit moved above them, the Spirit of whom he says elsewhere through the prophet David: Send forth your Spirit, and they shall be created. And elsewhere he also said of him: For I shall see the heavens, the work of your fingers. For God did not make heaven and earth with bodily fingers, but by the sevenfold grace of the Spirit, by that finger, namely, of which you read in the gospel: But if I cast out demons by the finger of God. Elsewhere he called this finger the Spirit, as you have it: But if I cast out demons by the Spirit of God. If, then, the Spirit is the finger of God, since the Son is the arm of God, surely the Spirit, working together with the Father and the Son in one working, made heaven and earth. For the Son spoke of a finger precisely so as to express the unity of the Godhead as of one body. So if great power founded heaven, surely great wisdom founded heaven, for it is written: In wisdom you have made all things.

We have learned, then, what great power is; let us now gather what great mercy is. If great power made the heavens, then great mercy too must come from heaven, and great justice must come from heaven; for justice looked down from heaven, and mercy came from heaven. So great mercy came about, because the Word became flesh and dwelt among us. Great power made the heavens; great power bowed the heavens, as we read: And he bowed the heavens and came down. This shows that the Son of God was never without his divinity, not even when he lived among men; for though he took up what he was not, he did not cease to be what he was. So when it is said, And he bowed the heavens and came down, he seems not so much to have come down from heaven as to have come down together with heaven. For when the Father spoke to the Son as he stood on earth, and angels ministered to him, the Son of God seems not so much to have changed his seat as to have carried it with him. So we have learned that mercy is great.

So if coming down from heaven is great mercy, we must distinguish and understand what the multitude of mercies is. For the psalm goes on: And according to the multitude of your mercies blot out my iniquity. The two verses do not mean the same thing. The first refers to the incarnation, while the one that follows seems to refer to the injuries the Son of God endured in the flesh: that he fasted, hungered, wept, was scourged, was crucified, died and was buried. These are the marks of the flesh, not of the Godhead. And it was necessary that a multitude of mercies should drive away the multitude of hardships, through the struggle of the Lord's passion, which was to benefit us.

For he was not blotting out his own sins, since he had committed no sin; but because he was made sin, our sins had to be blotted out, as David said: "Blot out my iniquity." What does "blot out" mean? Let us look at this word; it is not idle. Indeed, elsewhere too he says: "I am, I am he who blots out your iniquities, and I will not remember them." There are surely certain sores of sin deeply imprinted on our conscience, and certain weals on our minds and souls, which are covered over by the sores of our errors. Guilt, then, has its own characters and letters, by which it is betrayed. This we do not invent by our own ingenuity; we set our seal on it by prophetic authority. It is written, then; and see where it is written. "On the breast," it says, "of your heart"; that is, the record of guilt is written in the very place where the form of virtue is also written, "not on tablets of stone but on fleshly tablets of the heart." But good things are inscribed "not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God," whereas evil things are written "with an iron stylus and a diamond point." The writing is much like the punishment of sin. The one is written with an iron stylus; the other is restrained with a rod of iron, as it is written: "You shall rule them with a rod of iron." Quite different is that other rod: "an upright rod, the rod of your kingdom." The one restrains the guilty with punishment; the other governs the innocent by its rule. So guilt is written; let us see where. Not outside, but within, in your heart and in your breast. For just as "the word is near, in your mouth and in your heart," so in unbelievers a figure is impressed on the heart itself: the image of sin and error. Within, then, is guilt; within is virtue. And so the Lord says, "I perceive that virtue has gone out from me," to show that good things proceed from within, and likewise that evil things come forth from within. "For it is not what enters the mouth," he says, "that defiles a man, but what comes out of the mouth." For thoughts proceed from your heart; so beware lest evil thoughts come forth from your heart which may later convict and accuse you. For God needs no witnesses or proofs to convict you; your own guilt accuses and betrays you.

Hence David rightly says in this psalm: "My sin is ever before me." Woe is me, that I long to hide and cannot hide! For how shall I hide, when I carry the evidence of my sins written on my breast? On that day of judgment each person's breast will be laid bare, his conscience bearing witness to all, and his thoughts accusing or even defending one another, "on the day when God will judge the secrets of men." What shame there will be when what we thought hidden begins to be disclosed to all, when the image of each one's sin begins to reveal itself, so that each is convicted by the record of his own crime! What shame, when you see preferred before you the one you judged contemptible in this world—that servant of yours, the one you thought foolish and incapable by the cunning standards of this world—and you find him honored for the riches of his simplicity! So while we live, let us flee to him who can blot out sin. Do not be afraid because it is written with an iron stylus and a diamond point—for he broke the gates of iron and adamant—and do not fear to confess your guilt.

David confessed; he acknowledged his iniquity, he acknowledged his error, and so he says: "For I acknowledge my iniquity." David acknowledges, and you do not? David confesses, and you deny? Paul cries out that he is guilty, and you claim to be innocent? Is there not, then, the greatest cause for shame, when our fellowship is mixed up with so many sins? Yet if we pursue the desire to amend.... [?] Nor again should you be afraid that the confession of guilt will be held against you for punishment. For God, good and merciful, is accustomed not only to pardon the guilt of those who confess but also to bestow rewards on those who amend, provided each asks to be forgiven what he understands is not hidden. Tell your iniquities, then, that you may be justified. That is the voice of God, who wishes to pardon; that is the voice of God, who promises that he is willing to blot out your sin.

"Against you," he says, "have I sinned, and done evil before you"; that is: even if men do not see, yet you see; even if men cannot judge me, since they share in sins, you are nevertheless the judge of each one, you who have no share in sins. However deeply harmful thoughts may lie hidden in the inmost heart, they are before you, who can say: "Why do you think evil in your hearts?" It is, of course, Christ who says this. He, then, who knows what is written in the heart can blot out whatever is inscribed in the heart. To him holy David confesses that he sinned not only in himself but also in the first man, when the divine commands were violated.

Here we may observe, dearly beloved brethren, how all heresies, while attacking one another, run back into one another. Thus the Arians, by separating the power of the Father and the Son, rush so wildly to the end of their argument that their assertion coincides with that of the Manichees; for these say that there is one God of the Old Testament and another of the New. This profane assertion the holy Church condemns, for it reads of one God: "for there is one God the Father, from whom are all things, and we in him, and one Lord Jesus, through whom are all things, and we through him." Surely the power of the Father and the Son is declared to be almighty and one, so that we neither sever the Father from the grace of the New Testament nor, again, separate the Son from the establishing of the world.

Next, let us consider whether the same God is the founder of both testaments. Surely we all sinned in the first man, and through the succession of nature the succession of guilt too has been passed on from one to all. Against whom, then, did I sin—against the Father or against the Son? Surely against him who lent me what I sinned by not keeping. Man was commanded to taste of everything that was in paradise but not to touch the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. Adam, then, is in each one of us. For in him human nature transgressed, since through one man sin passed to all. I see the sum lent to me; I see the debt of transgression I have contracted by tasting what was forbidden and prohibited. Hence I owe interest on the capital entrusted to me, because I could not keep the loan of the heavenly commandments with unblemished faith. We have recognized the loan; let us also recognize the lender.

It is surely the lender's right both to demand payment and to remit it. And so the one who remits is the same who has the right to demand. When, therefore, Christ has said to me in the gospel, "Your sins are forgiven you," do I not understand the one I recognize as the arbiter of pardon to be the same as the lord of the capital? Or if the Father lent and the Son remitted—not through unity, as we say, but, as the Arians assert, through difference of power—did one God lend and another remit? This is where they end up, so that they do not escape the faithlessness of the Manichees. Then, by saying that one God is good, let them see into what snares of their own madness they fall. If he who lent is good, how is he who remitted not good? So let the Arians share the lot of those with whose assertion they agree.

Nor is it surprising if one who has once begun to stray from the truth entangles himself in the knots of another's error. And so there is one principle that destroys the engines of all the heretics: that we believe the Trinity to be of one power, majesty and might, and therefore neither separate the Father from what the Son did nor sever the Son from what the Father commanded. In this way we shall not introduce one God of the Old Testament and another of the New; rather, through the unity of power, the Son will be understood in the Father and the Father in the Son, and the Son lends in the Father and the Father remits in the Son. For the Father also forgives sin; that the Son has forgiven we have already said.

Learn that the Father also forgives: "Forgive us our debts," he says, "as we also forgive our debtors." Surely the Son says this to the Father in our person. And he does not say it as though he himself could not forgive, but he says it so that you may understand the unity of power.

Then, if you are looking for authority in the Son: "You are already clean," he says, "because of the word which I have spoken to you." He forgives by word, he forgives by command, but he forgives with reason, saying: "Go, and from now on see that you sin no more." You have his authority, for he pardoned what was past; you have his judgment, for he laid down a rule for the future.
